extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and students of rhetoric/classical style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing elevated, 'sublime' prose and oratory—covering use of metaphor, hyperbole, diction, rhythm/harmony, arrangement, and the balance between lofty genius and technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness can redeem vulgar terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse or 'vulgar' expressions (e.g., “he destroyed himself”; “continued fighting ... until he was entirely hacked to pieces”) may strike the common reader, but their vulgarity is redeemed by their expressiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coarse language only when its force and expressiveness serve the passage; striking, vivid terms can be justified by their expressive power. Anti-pattern: gratuitous vulgarity that lacks expressive necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of metaphors (but follow occasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many critics advise not more than two or three metaphors combined in the same place, but the proper number must be determined by the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In calmer passages, avoid packing many metaphors together; in outbursts of passion or descriptive sequences, larger clusters of metaphors are allowable or even necessary. Use judgement based on the emotional intensity and purpose of the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soften harsh metaphors when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Harsh or bold metaphors may be softened with qualifying phrases such as 'so to say', 'as it were', 'if I may be permitted the expression', 'if so bold a term is allowable' to anticipate criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such hedges to forestall objections to daring language. But if strong feeling and sublimity sweep the reader along, these softeners may be unnecessary. Balance mitigation with the risk of weakening the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion and unaffected sublimity mitigate excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-timed displays of strong feeling and unaffected sublimity serve as native antidotes to the number and boldness of metaphors, carrying the hearer so he will not pause to criticise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When genuine passion drives a passage, daring metaphors feel appropriate and are less likely to be judged as excess. Anti-pattern: forced passion used to excuse florid ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use close, continuous metaphors in descriptive and familiar topics
rubrics_metrics.description: In description and treatment of familiar subjects, a close and continuous series of metaphors gives distinctness and vivid delineation (examples: Xenophon, Plato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For anatomy, characterization, or vivid images, chaining metaphors can create a life-like picture. Ensure metaphors remain coherent and contribute to a unified image rather than confusing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the tendency of figurative language to excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Figurative language has a constant tendency towards excess (e.g., Plato sometimes carried away by 'frenzy of language' into intemperate metaphors and inflated allegory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for over-elaboration and inflated allegory. Excess may draw hostile criticism and reduce clarity. Revise to remove overstrained or absurd conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer loftiness with faults over faultless mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: A sublime writer who occasionally errs is often preferable to a flawless writer of only moderate excellence; loftier excellences should be ranked over numerous lesser merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value grand, original thinking and emotional power even when accompanied by occasional slips. Anti-pattern: prioritizing mechanical correctness at the expense of ambition and grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge success merely by number of merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of accomplishments is not the true standard; loftiness and supreme qualities (e.g., Demosthenes' passion and power) can outweigh many lesser excellences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the impact and height of qualities rather than counting polished but minor virtues. Example contrast: Hyperides (many varied merits) vs. Demosthenes (fewer but overwhelming powers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole must not be overstrained; best when arising naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole spoils its effect when overstrained or obvious; it is most effective when it grows naturally out of circumstances or appears 'in disguise'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbole that is credible within context—especially in scenes of frenzy or crisis where extreme expressions gain plausibility (examples: Thucydides' massacre descriptions, Herodotus at Thermopylae). Avoid flourishes that signal unreliability or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make hyperbole credible via emotional context or humour
rubrics_metrics.description: In passions verging on frenzy, licence of language is pardoned; in comic passages, extravagance can gain credence by humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage emotional intensity or comic tone to justify improbable or exaggerated claims. Conversely, don't use hyperbole to bluff or to disguise weak factual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony/arrangement of words elevates style
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arrangement of words—harmony—has a natural power to win, delight, exalt the soul and sway the heart; modulation, cadence, and placement of phrases (example: Demosthenes' decree compared to 'a cloud') create sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange words for rhythmic and sonic effect; reserve key phrases or place words to maximize tonal impact. Small transpositions or syllabic changes can cripple or enhance grandeur. Consider meter, cadence, and final positioning of phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhythmic and metric modulation judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific rhythmic shaping (e.g., dactylic measure, delaying certain words) intensifies grandeur; shortening or elongating syllables alters the perceived majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to length and stress patterns: sometimes a heavy measure or final-reserved phrase heightens effect; inappropriate abbreviations or elongations can dissipate force. Avoid monotonous, dance-like rhythms (pyrrhics/trochees) that distract from meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose clauses as organic wholes (rounded periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause or period gains sublimity from joint contributions of many particulars; elements joined in an organic whole, compacted by harmony and rounding of the period, gain power of tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft sentences so that parts reinforce the whole—use balance, cadence, and strategic pauses. Avoid chopping ideas into disjointed fragments that lose cumulative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-rhythmical, effeminate, or hurried movement
rubrics_metrics.description: An over-rhythmical passage (regular dance-like cadence) becomes tiresome and reduces dignity; splitting sentences into many small, crowded words produces a petty, undignified tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary rhythmic patterns; do not let cadence overshadow sense. Ensure rhythm serves meaning rather than becoming an end in itself. Anti-pattern: predictably metrical prose that prompts listeners to 'beat time' with the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cramping diction and over-compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-compression—cutting words too short—dwarfs style and fritters away force; concise should mean direct, not pruned of sense; over-extension likewise makes style lifeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for balance: be direct and concise but allow sufficient breadth for clarity and power. Watch for excessive brevity that sacrifices nuance and for verbosity that relaxes tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean, petty or sordid words in lofty passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of mean or vulgar expressions (e.g., 'having seethed', 'wore away', 'unwelcome end', juxtaposing 'panniers' with 'jewelled bowls') degrades a lofty subject and produces blemishes on diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep diction appropriate to subject: avoid mixing petty, everyday terms with grand themes. Either use broad, elevated strokes for magnificence or, if specificity is necessary, deploy elevated specificities or grouped generalities rather than trivial particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give grand scenes broad, elevated summary rather than petty details
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing magnificent scenes, avoid descending into incongruous petty enumerations; prefer generalizing phrases or a few noble details rather than lists of trivial items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace exact petty items with grouped or elevated descriptions (e.g., 'long train of baggage animals' or 'piles of grain and choicest delicacies') to preserve dignity. Anti-pattern: mixing 'panniers and spices and bags' among treasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sordid/despicable detail unless absolutely necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stoop to sordid or despicable particulars in sublimer efforts unless urgent necessity demands it; utterance should be worthy of theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceal grossness where possible (take lesson from nature's concealment of rude parts); use low detail only when it serves an important rhetorical or realistic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use art to ally with nature—craft tempers genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Art (craft) should be called in as an ally to natural genius: avoidance of error is usually the gift of art, while high, unequal excellence is the attribute of genius; their combined resources approach perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate technical skill—judgement, arrangement, diction—to temper and realize the ambitions of genius. Balance bold inspiration with disciplined workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and moral context shapes rhetorical excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of society (e.g., corruption, greed) and the writer's purposes shape the growth or decay of genius and rhetorical excellence; true sublimity arises from nobler aims rather than servile flattery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for nobility of purpose: cultivate impartiality, seriousness, and pursuit of what is 'diviner' rather than pandering to appetite or applause. Anti-pattern: rhetorical skill devoted solely to flattery or gain, which undermines lasting greatness.
